paragraphs.heading: A muscular bag
paragraphs.text: The stomach is a hollow, muscular organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract, found in people and many other animals, some invertebrates among them. The Ancient Greek name for it was gaster, which is why medical words about the stomach use gastric. It has a widened shape and is a vital organ of the digestive system. In people it sits between the esophagus and the small intestine, in the upper left part of the abdomen.

paragraphs.heading: What it does
paragraphs.text: Digestion in the stomach is called the gastric phase. It follows the cephalic phase, when seeing and smelling food and chewing it act as triggers. In the stomach, food is broken down chemically by digestive enzymes and gastric acid that the stomach releases. The stomach also helps regulate the gut microbiota, which affects digestion and overall health.

paragraphs.heading: Two gates
paragraphs.text: Two sphincters keep the stomach's contents inside. The lower esophageal sphincter sits where the esophagus joins the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter sits where the stomach meets the duodenum, the opening stretch of the small intestine and its shortest part. The pyloric sphincter controls how partly digested food, called chyme, moves into the duodenum. From there, peristalsis moves it through the rest of the intestines.

paragraphs.heading: Size and shape
paragraphs.text: The stomach can stretch, and normally holds about a litre of food. Its shape depends on how full it is and on how full its neighbours are, such as the colon. Empty, it is roughly J-shaped, partly full it takes a shape called pyriform, and in obese people it lies more horizontally. A newborn baby's stomach holds only about 30 millilitres, while an adult's maximum is 2 to 4 litres, and up to 15 litres has been seen in extreme cases.

paragraphs.heading: Four regions
paragraphs.text: The human stomach is divided into four sections, in order: the cardia, the fundus, the body and the pylorus. The cardia is a very small region around the opening from the esophagus. The fundus, from the Latin for bottom, forms the upper curved part. The body, or corpus, is the main central region, and the pylorus, from the Greek for gatekeeper, joins the stomach to the duodenum at the pyloric sphincter.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of the wall
paragraphs.text: Like the rest of the gut wall, the stomach wall is built in layers. From the inside out they are the mucosa, submucosa, muscular layer, subserosa and serosa. The mucosa is the mucous membrane lining the stomach, and beneath it the submucosa is made of fibrous connective tissue.
